Article Title: Jensen Huang remembers Windows early days, crediting Microsoft, says that 'Nvidia was founded because of Windows'; CEO Satya Nadella jokes: If you could just do a little transfer of...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang and Satya Nadella relive the Windows 95 days.

Windows 95 and DirectX gave Nvidia's GPUs a way into the PC

A four-year-old conversation between Huang and Nadella led to RTX Spark

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said his company owes its existence to Microsoft's operating system. Speaking on stage at Microsoft's Windows and Surface event in San Francisco on October 7, Huang told the audience that "Nvidia was founded because of Windows," and traced a line from Windows 3.1 in 1992 to the GPUs that now power much of the AI industry.Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, sitting next to him, had a quick reply. "If you could just do a little transfer of market cap back to me," he joked, a nod to how far Nvidia's valuation has climbed. Huang shot back: "I do that every day." The conversation, hosted by Sriram Krishnan, former senior policy adviser for AI at the White House, came right after Microsoft unveiled the Surface Laptop Ultra and a range of laptops built on Nvidia's new RTX Spark chip.Huang went back to late 1992, when Windows 3.1 was showing what a personal computer could become. He admitted he had never seen a PC at the time, having mostly worked on workstations, file servers and the supercomputers used to design chips. He and his co-founders imagined a PC with 3D graphics that could play games, work as a workstation and be used to design things.Windows 95 then made it possible to connect a GPU to a PC, and DirectX, through its Direct3D API, let applications use what the GPU could do.With DirectX 8, Huang said, Nvidia and Microsoft co-invented the first programmable GPU with programmable shaders. A few steps later, that work evolved into CUDA, Nvidia's parallel computing platform."If not for Windows, there would be no GeForce," Huang said. Without GeForce, he added, there would be no CUDA, and AI researchers like Andrew Ng would not have found a computer to do deep learning on.Nadella called the story "the history of computing in some sense" and credited Huang as the most consistent voice on what accelerated computing could become. He recalled an early Azure deal to scale high-performance computing in the cloud, which led Microsoft to build the supercomputer it later offered to OpenAI. When Sam Altman asked if Microsoft had the compute, Nadella's answer was "yeah, maybe."That partnership eventually brought the two back to the PC. Huang said they discussed how to put every major tool, from Blender to Adobe and Autodesk apps, on the same machine as AI agents. "By the way, took four years," Nadella added.The result is RTX Spark, which Huang said took over 4,000 engineering years and has been tested on more than 1,200 applications. RTX Spark laptops from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, MSI and Microsoft's own Surface are now up for preorder and begin shipping on October 16.As the session wrapped up, Huang summed up the relationship himself: "Windows has been with me for 34 years, it looks like it's going to be with me for 34 more."
Article Summary: Jensen Huang: "N Nvidia was founded because of Windows" He traced a line from Windows 3.1 in 1992 to the GPUs that now power much of the AI industry. Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella discussed how to put every major tool on the same machine as AI agents.

Article Title: In 2019, the research company that called now bankrupt WeWork 'most ridiculous IPO of 2019' has same 'most-ridiculous' description for Anthropic IPO, and reason is ...
Article Text:
Anthropic’s valuation expectations at the centre of concerns

A mixed track record

What the firm hasn't seen

As AI giant Anthropic moves toward a highly anticipated public listing that could value the company at nearly $2 trillion, independent research firm New Constructs has issued a scathing assessment, calling it the "most ridiculous IPO of 2026" and drawing comparisons with WeWork, whose failed public offering became one of the biggest corporate collapses of the last decade. According to a report by CNBC, the criticism carries some weight on Wall Street because New Constructs used the same description for WeWork in 2019, months before the office-sharing company abandoned its IPO plans amid investor backlash over its finances and governance. WeWork eventually filed for bankruptcy in 2023. According to a CNBC report, the research firm's latest report argues that Anthropic's proposed valuation presents an even bigger risk for investors than WeWork's offering did.New Constructs estimates that to justify a $2 trillion valuation, Anthropic would need to earn twice what Nvidia, the world's most valuable tech company, earned over its past four quarters. Nvidia's net income over that period topped $190 billion. The firm pointed to Anthropic's reported finances. According to Reuters, which cited a leaked copy of the company's prospectus, Anthropic had revenue of $4.6 billion in 2025 and a net loss of $42 billion.Those losses, along with growing competition from open-source models, led the firm to a blunt conclusion: "We don't think Anthropic has a viable business." The report argues that closed models were always going to struggle to turn a profit once open-source alternatives arrived.It also argued that the offering's purpose is not to create wealth for public-market investors but to give Anthropic's Wall Street backers liquidity. And it said Anthropic's own warning that AI could pose a "catastrophic or existential risk to humanity" is another reason for investors to stay away. The firm acknowledged Anthropic's value beyond the balance sheet. "While Anthropic offers more to society than WeWork ever did," it wrote, the $2 trillion valuation makes the IPO a far bigger risk and potentially a "far bigger rip off of US capital markets. "David Trainer, New Constructs' founder and CEO, has built a reputation as a bear on IPOs, and he has sometimes been right. WeWork had been privately valued at $47 billion when New Constructs published its report. Six weeks later, WeWork pulled its IPO amid weak demand and criticism of its financials, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2023.The firm was also bearish on Allbirds' 2021 offering. The shoe company reached a $4.1 billion valuation on its first day on the Nasdaq. Earlier this year it sold its assets to American Exchange Group for an estimated $39 million and pivoted to AI.The firm has also been wrong. Its "most ridiculous" pick for 2020 was DoorDash, which it called "similarly disadvantaged" to WeWork. DoorDash jumped on its first day of trading in December 2020, with a market cap above $60 billion, and is now worth about $83 billion. Trainer acknowledged in a 2021 CNBC interview that "crazy stuff happens" and that the firm does not always get it right. "I can't let that bother me," he said then. "I have to stay true to what I think is right."Anthropic has not made its prospectus public, so New Constructs has not seen the actual filing. The firm relied on reported figures, including from the New York Times, which reported in September that Anthropic was on pace for $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026. Anthropic said at the end of July that its annualized revenue run rate had risen sevenfold year over year to $65 billion."While we were not fortunate enough to be one of the few to whom Anthropic's S-1 was selectively disclosed," the firm wrote, the reports of leaked financials "reveal more than enough" to judge the risks.
Article Summary: Anthropic is preparing for a highly anticipated public listing that could value the company at nearly $2 trillion. Independent research firm New Constructs has issued a scathing assessment, calling it the "most ridiculous IPO of 2026" The report argues that Anthropic's proposed valuation presents an even bigger risk for investors than WeWork's offering did.

Article Title: After $6.25 billion 'gift' to Trump Accounts, Michael Dell's wife Susan Dell makes an 'appeal' to parents and grandparents, says: There is money in ...
Article Text:
Michael Dell and wife Susan Dell

What are Trump Accounts

Michael and Susan Dell donated $250 each to first 25 million Trump accounts

Michael Dell’s wife Susan Dell has made an ‘appeal’ to parents and grandparents to claim their child’s money in Trump accounts. The couple attended a press conference alongside President Donald Trump at the Oval Office celebrating the automatic enrollment of millions of American children in the ‘Trump Accounts’. “We believe in you, and we want you to dream big because we know you can make your dreams come true,” Susan Dell said adding “So parents and grandparents, please claim your child's account. These accounts are ready. They're waiting for you, and they have money in them.”The move comes months after Michael and Susan Dell committed $6.25 billion to fund “Trump Accounts” for children in the US. Announcing the donation last year, Michael Dell said: "We've seen what happens when a child gets even a small financial headstart - their world expands".Trump Accounts are new, tax-advantaged investment accounts for children in the US, created under the 2025 federal tax law known as the Working Families Tax Cuts. Legally, they are a type of traditional IRA created under new Section 530A of the tax code. Eligible US-citizen children born between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2028 can receive a one-time $1,000 Treasury contribution, if the required election is made.IRSThe basic idea is to give children an investment asset early in life, allowing money to potentially grow through compound returns over many years. The Trump administration describes the programme as a way to give children a financial head start and encourage wider participation in investing.On July 4, as America marked its 250th birthday, the Dell Technologies founder and his wife Susan Dell gave $250 each to the first 25 million qualifying American children who sign up for a 'Trump Accounts’. Dell made the announcement on X, formerly Twitter, framing it as a "public-private partnership" that hands the next generation "a real stake in our economy." The couple had already pledged more than $6 billion to the programme back in December, so Saturday's post added a number to a commitment already made.“Today, on America's 250th birthday, Susan and I are celebrating by giving $250 each to the first 25 million qualifying American children who sign up for their @InvestAmerica24 @TrumpAccounts. This makes every child a shareholder in the greatest prosperity-creating engine the world has ever known—American capitalism. Through this public-private partnership, we're giving the next generation a real stake in our economy and a path to the American Dream: education, a first home, starting a business, and building lasting wealth. It unites us all in hope and optimism for every child's future. Happy 250th Birthday, America!,” the post then said.
Article Summary: Michael and Susan Dell donated $250 each to first 25 million Trump accounts. Trump Accounts are new, tax-advantaged investment accounts for children in the US, created under the 2025 federal tax law known as the Working Families Tax Cuts. The couple had already pledged more than $6 billion to the programme back in December.

Article Title: Nuuk partners with EPACK Durable to manufacture air fryers, air circulator fans in India
Article Text:
Focus on scaling high-quality products

EPACK expands SDA portfolio

Direct-to-consumer home appliance brand Nuuk has partnered with EPACK Durable Limited, one of India's leading original design manufacturers (ODMs) of consumer durables, to manufacture select small domestic appliances, including air circulator fans and air fryers. The partnership is aimed at strengthening Nuuk's manufacturing capabilities as it scales its product portfolio, while also expanding EPACK Durable's presence in the fast-growing small domestic appliances (SDA) segment. The companies said the collaboration combines Nuuk's design-led product development approach with EPACK Durable's manufacturing expertise.According to the companies, the agreement forms part of Nuuk's broader strategy to deepen its manufacturing ecosystem through partnerships with specialised production companies. The arrangement is expected to help the brand scale production while maintaining a focus on product quality, functionality and consumer-centric design.Nuuk, which has positioned itself as a new-age consumer appliances brand, said the collaboration will support its efforts to build products tailored to Indian consumers while strengthening its commitment to local manufacturing."Our partnership with EPACK Durable brings together our product and design orientation with deep manufacturing capabilities in the small domestic appliances category," said Gazal Kalra and Shalabh Gupta, co-founders of Nuuk.They added that the partnership would allow the company to expand with greater scale while remaining focused on quality and functionality.For EPACK Durable, the agreement broadens its engagement with emerging consumer appliance brands and further strengthens its SDA manufacturing portfolio. "We are pleased to partner with Nuuk and support the brand with our manufacturing capabilities across the consumer appliances segment," said Ajay DD Singhania, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of EPACK Durable. He said the company remains focused on building long-term relationships with brands through manufacturing scale, product capabilities and execution strength.EPACK Durable currently manufactures products across categories including room air conditioners, small domestic appliances, large domestic appliances and components through its manufacturing facilities in India. The company serves a range of consumer durable brands across the country.The companies said the partnership could create opportunities for broader collaboration across India's consumer appliances ecosystem in the future, combining product-led innovation with domestic manufacturing expertise as demand for locally manufactured appliances continues to grow.
Article Summary: Nuuk has partnered with EPACK Durable Limited, one of India's leading original design manufacturers. The partnership is aimed at strengthening Nuuk's manufacturing capabilities as it scales its product portfolio. EPACK expands its presence in the fast-growing small domestic appliances (SDA) segment.

Article Title: What Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees in first townhall since hundreds of layoffs at Microsoft's gaming division
Article Text:
Why do we exist? We exist to be where the world plays, we will know when we have a billion daily active people, and we have a right to win because we're now focused on our fans and franchises

“We're making the right decisions to reinvest in the business, after an all time low, we've started to return to growth, more than 2 to 3 times what we were, and we expect that continue.”

‘Four Cs’ and renewed console commitment

“We are moving to a family of devices for Gen-10. There is not one device that fits all. We will certainly have a great console first, but we also know that many players will be on the go. There are some things that we are the best in the world to manufacture, and there are other things that we will partner on... The operating system is starting to look really good. We're very excited about this.”

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly addressed company staff in her first company-wide town hall since sweeping summer layoffs hit Microsoft’s gaming division, laying out a comprehensive roadmap to stabilise the brand, committing to traditional console players and preparing for next-generation hardware. Citing a transcript of an internal gathering that followed a turbulent stretch marked by hundreds of job cuts, studio divestments and internal closures, a report by Windows Central says that Sharma acknowledged that Xbox entered 2026 facing severe headwinds, with user engagement hours, active player counts and top-line revenue all sliding downward.She pointed out that the division’s prior subscription approach, which previously led to removing Call of Duty from standard tiers alongside major price cuts, pushed Xbox’s balance sheet into what she termed a “freefall.” Now Sharma has stated that player hours have steadied, while first-party publishing output has bounced back:,” Sharma reportedly told staff.Highlighting internal metrics, Sharma noted that first-party game (games that Xbox owns and publishes) momentum is up by two to three times over recent historical lows.She cited early wins from titles like Gears of War: E-Day, Minecraft Dungeons 2, and World of Warcraft Forever, adding that positive public sentiment around the Xbox brand has climbed by 30% over the past year.Sharma framed the division’s operational recovery around four core pillars: Core, Content, Creation and Connection. Despite broader industry data showing flatlining console hardware adoption worldwide, Sharma argued that Xbox cannot justify expanding into wider segments if it fails to take care of its primary base. Xbox must invest more heavily in home consoles, asserting the company lacks “the right to grow beyond console” if it does not properly support its most dedicated audience.Moreover, the team is said to be prioritising current-gen hardware features, including Xbox Cloud Gaming upgrades, an expanding disc-to-digital migration program, and the continued reach of Xbox Play Anywhere. Sharma also signaled that Xbox Game Pass will introduce greater customisation, allowing users to pick and choose specific content packages rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach.Looking ahead, Sharma confirmed early architectural details regarding Xbox’s tenth-generation platform, internally codenamed Xbox Helix. Article Title: After claiming it solved 90-year-old Maths problem that made Mathematicians around the world angry with Sam Altman's company, OpenAI now says it has solved more than 350 such problems
Article Text:
Inside the 700-paper Math drop

Just weeks after claiming to have solved a 90-year-old Millennium Prize Problem that sparked outrage across the global mathematical community, OpenAI has published hundreds of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model. The Sam Altman-led lab released an open repository containing 722 research manuscripts organised into 372 distinct problem families. The documents cover a vast array of disciplines, including number theory and algebraic geometry, and claim major advances tied to three of the five remaining Millennium Prize Problems, including the legendary Riemann hypothesis.The release comes after a wave of skepticism from mathematicians, who voiced deep concerns about how machine-generated mathematics could disrupt their ancient field. This time, the company said that it has consulted an advisory group on mathematics and AI.“We’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study, and we have drawn on their advice and public recommendations to inform how we release these results,” the company added.Behind closed doors, OpenAI continued running its models on open research challenges after standard mathematical benchmarks became saturated.That left the company with an unusual challenge: how to package and release a massive volume of synthetic math to a skeptical academic world.According to OpenAI’s documentation, the repository features 722 manuscripts across 372 families with each family group containing primary findings alongside companion arguments, corollaries and alternative proof strategies.OpenAI acknowledged that not every paper is completely verified or paired with computer-checked formal code, and to build trust, the company is publishing formalisations in Lean (a programming language designed to let computers verify proof logic) and promised to add more over time.OpenAI also conceded that unformalised results may contain errors, pledging to patch identified flaws quickly while exploring community-hosted repositories. In a bid to demonstrate scientific openness, OpenAI shared technical data detailing the resources required to generate the proofs.The company revealed that the average mathematical result consumed the compute equivalent of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking time. Alongside the raw papers, the lab published 10 breakdowns of the model's internal reasoning chains, estimates of total compute expenditures, and aggregate statistics tracking the total volume of attempted problems.
Article Summary: OpenAI has published hundreds of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model. The Sam Altman-led lab released an open repository containing 722 research manuscripts organised into 372 distinct problem families. The release comes after a wave of skepticism from mathematicians, who voiced deep concerns about how machine-generated mathematics could disrupt their field.

Article Title: Months after Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman predicted AI will automate most White Collar jobs in 18 months, he now agrees with Nobel winner Daron Acemoglu that AI won't take your job anytime soon,
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO predicted AI will automate most White Collar jobs

What Daron Acemoglu says AI job fears are exaggerated

Policy proposals

Just months after warning that artificial intelligence could automate most white-collar tasks within 12 to 18 months, Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft AI, is now promoting a much more gradual vision of the technology's impact on jobs, backing Nobel Prize-winning economist Daron Acemoglu's argument that AI will replace only a small portion of human work over the next decade. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) highlighting an essay by Acemoglu in the inaugural issue of The Humanist Review, a magazine published by Microsoft AI, Suleyman said fears that AI will rapidly eliminate jobs are overblown and that the focus should shift towards building systems that help workers become more productive rather than replacing them.In an interview with the Financial Times in February, Suleyman said most, if not all, white-collar tasks would be fully automated by AI within 12 to 18 months. He named accounting, legal work, marketing and project management as vulnerable. The prediction spread widely, and Sen. Bernie Sanders called it an "economic earthquake" if it came true.Suleyman's latest post points the other way. He wrote that in ten years only 5% of what humans do will be replaced by AI, citing Acemoglu's essay in the first issue of The Humanist Review, a new magazine from Microsoft AI (MAI) about the future of AI.The post does not say whether Suleyman is revising his February forecast, and Microsoft AI did not immediately respond to questions about it.Sharing the essay, Suleyman highlighted Acemoglu's argument that AI will not take people's jobs anytime soon and that only around 5% of human tasks are likely to be replaced by AI over the next 10 years. According to the economist, about 52% of Americans are worried about AI's impact on employment, but those concerns are influencing AI development in the wrong direction by encouraging efforts focused on automation rather than augmentation.Instead, Acemoglu argues that companies should develop "pro-worker AI" tools that improve employees' capabilities and help them perform their jobs more effectively.Acemoglu argues the industry is making a mistake by trying to make AI mimic human intelligence, which he says is fundamentally different from machine intelligence. He wants developers to build "pro-worker AI" that makes people better at their jobs and gives them new skills. He says such tools are feasible with today's models, and gives teaching as an example. An AI tool could flag which parts of a curriculum students struggle with and suggest how a teacher might regroup the class, rather than trying to replace the teacher.He says four forces have pushed the industry toward automation:1. Tech companies' existing business models are built on selling software to corporations and on digital advertising.2. A concentrated market leaves little room for new entrants to try alternatives.3. A "nuts and bolts" coordination problem leaves firms and developers each waiting for the other to demand something different.4. The influence of the AGI idea and "human parity" as the measure of success.Acemoglu says the US tax code should be changed. He notes that labor faces an effective marginal rate of more than 25%, while capital faces a rate close to zero, which effectively subsidizes automation. He also calls for stronger antitrust enforcement, noting that the seven largest tech companies make up 60% of the Nasdaq. Other proposals include a digital advertising tax, small government programs to demonstrate pro-worker tools, and a functioning market for high-quality data.The essay does not spare Suleyman's industry, including Microsoft. Acemoglu names Microsoft among the seven giants and notes that it acquired Nuance, the owner of the Dragon voice-recognition software, which he says neglected consumer products. The magazine is published by Microsoft AI.
Article Summary: Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft AI, said in February that most white-collar tasks would be automated by AI within 12 to 18 months. In a post on Twitter, he said fears that AI will rapidly eliminate jobs are overblown and that the focus should shift towards building systems that help workers become more productive rather than replacing them. In ten years only 5% of what humans do will be replaced by AI.

Article Title: As AI fear spreads across America, a Republican state becomes first to allow AI doctor; that critics say paves way to jobs in medicine getting automated with AI
Article Text:
AI generated image for representation

Utah becomes first state to allow AI prescriptions

"AI will matter most in healthcare when it helps people get care they otherwise would not receive,"

How the AI doctor works

AI replacing doctors remains a concern

"People are right to worry about

AI in medicine

that nobody can control. This program was built to be the opposite,"

"The AI can't improvise. It can only choose from a short list of physician-approved topical treatments. The moment a patient falls outside those limits, it stops and hands them to a doctor."

Utah has already tested AI for prescriptions

Utah is allowing an AI system to prescribe medicines. As AI fears spread across the US, the Republican-led state has become the first in the country to approve an AI system that can issue initial prescriptions, raising fresh questions about whether parts of medicine could eventually be automated. The pilot, launched by Nolla Health, currently covers acne treatment for adults through its Nolla Derm app.The system assesses patients using a questionnaire and facial scan before selecting treatments from a limited list approved by physicians. While the company says the programme is designed to expand access to care rather than replace doctors, critics worry about AI taking over medical decisions and potentially paving the way for greater automation of healthcare jobs.Nolla Health said it received regulatory approval following months of work with the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence and the Utah Medical Board. The company says the system is designed to address limited access to dermatology care. More than 80% of US counties are considered healthcare deserts, according to Nolla, while Utah has an estimated 100,000 people living with active acne.The company said the average dermatology wait time in Utah is 61 days, while 11 counties have no dermatologists.Luis Wenus, co-founder and CEO of Nolla Health, said the technology is intended to expand access rather than replace doctors.Wenus said.Patients aged 18 and above can use the Nolla Derm app by completing an informed consent process, a 10- to 15-minute questionnaire and a facial scan. The system analyses their acne and other skin characteristics, then creates a treatment plan. The service costs $4.99 a month.The AI cannot issue open-ended prescriptions. Instead, it can select from a limited list of physician-approved topical treatments. If it cannot confidently determine an appropriate treatment, it refers the patient to a licensed physician.The rollout will also introduce physician oversight in stages. For the first 100 patients, a doctor will review and approve every AI-generated prescription. For the first 500 prescriptions, the AI will issue prescriptions autonomously, while a physician reviews them daily. After that, doctors will review a weekly sample of prescriptions. Patients can also contact a licensed physician through the app.The Utah programme comes as debate continues in the US over whether AI could eventually automate parts of highly skilled professions, including medicine.Critics of AI in healthcare have raised concerns about the risks of relying on automated systems for medical decisions. The Utah pilot, however, is currently limited to acne, which Nolla describes as a well-understood, low-risk condition with established treatment pathways.Dr Zaid Fadul, Chief Medical Advisor at Nolla Health, said the system has been designed with limits.Fadul said.The acne programme is not Utah's first move toward using AI for prescription-related healthcare. The state launched another pilot in January that lets patients opt into an AI system to renew certain prescriptions after a doctor validates the initial action. The programme has faced criticism from some doctors who have questioned its safety.Nolla Health says its acne pilot is intended to complement physicians by handling routine cases, allowing dermatologists to focus on more complex patients.The Nolla Derm app has already been downloaded more than 175,000 times across 44 states. The Utah programme is currently a one-year pilot, with severe or complex acne cases referred to human doctors.
Article Summary: Utah becomes first state to allow AI prescriptions. The pilot, launched by Nolla Health, currently covers acne treatment for adults through its Nolla Derm app. The system assesses patients using a questionnaire and facial scan before selecting treatments from a limited list approved by physicians.

Article Title: As banks across the world 'dread' AI attacks, IMF MD Kristalina Georgieva says: Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is …
Article Text:
International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva

‘Global economy being pulled in opposite directions’

‘Inflation due to data centre expansion’

As financial institutions worldwide are getting increasingly worried over artificial intelligence (AI) and its risks, International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva delivered a reminder to world leaders: the technological shift is inevitable and its macroeconomic side effects can no longer be ignored. The IMF chief warned that while AI is rapidly determining the relative wealth and competitive edge of nations, it is also introducing new economic pressures that threaten an already sluggish decade of global growth.“Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here,” Georgieva declared during an address Wednesday (October 7) in Singapore, calling on governments to stop stalling on hard fiscal decisions as sovereign debt mounts worldwide.Speaking ahead of the upcoming IMF and World Bank annual meetings, Georgieva explained that international markets are caught in a dual squeeze. Firstly, she explains, a persistent negative energy supply shock driven by the war in the Gulf and crude oil above $100 a barrel, while tight refining capacity has driven retail diesel prices to all-time highs.The second reason is a massive, capital-intensive infrastructure surge centered on data centers and advanced computing.The collision of these two forces is creating sharp disparities around the world.Citing Georgieva, a report in CNBC says that the scale of data center construction is also fueling inflation anxieties across the US, Europe and Asia. She pointed out that alongside tariffs, defense budgets, and energy shocks, the AI building surge is actively inflationary.Georgieva also raised alarms over financial stability within the technology sector itself. While strong earnings have elevated equity valuations and created positive wealth effects, she cautioned that if corporate returns stumble, the debt taken on by hyperscalers and the heavy concentration of global wealth in US equities could amplify any shortfall into a far wider market shock.Referencing Amara’s Law, which posits that society tends to overestimate a technology’s impact in the short term while underestimating it in the long term, Georgieva highlighted the hazards of the current moment:“It is somewhere in the transition between today’s AI building boom and tomorrow’s arrival of AI’s benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk.”To safeguard the financial system, the IMF chief argued that strict regulatory oversight and supervisory guardrails must serve as the first line of defense.
Article Summary: International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva delivered a reminder to world leaders: the technological shift is inevitable. She warned that while AI is rapidly determining the relative wealth and competitive edge of nations, it is also introducing new economic pressures that threaten an already sluggish decade of global growth.

Gemini in Chrome Android India Auto Browse.

Auto browse shows its plan before it touches anything

Google has brought Gemini in Chrome to all Android users in India and switched on auto browse, the assistant's agentic mode, for paying subscribers on desktop and Android. Auto browse is limited to Google AI Pro and AI Ultra plans and lets Gemini carry out multi-step tasks on websites by itself, such as booking parking for an event, filling out a long form or ordering the week's groceries.The Android rollout follows the desktop launch in India earlier this year. On phones, the assistant does what it already does on a laptop. It can summarise a long article, answer questions about the page you're on and pull in Google apps like Calendar and Keep without switching tabs. Nano Banana image editing comes along too, so a picture on a web page can be reworked with a typed prompt. Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and several other Indian languages are supported.Before a task begins, Gemini lays out a plan for the user to check, including which sites it intends to use and what personal details it may share with them. It starts only after the user clicks Start Task, and works in a separate tab marked with an auto browse icon. Users can take over at any point, and Gemini stops to ask for confirmation before some sensitive steps. With permission, it can also sign in to sites through Google Password Manager without seeing the passwords.There are daily caps. AI Pro subscribers get up to 20 auto browse tasks a day, while Ultra users get 200. The feature does not work in Incognito mode.Google calls the agent experimental and says its models are trained to spot threats such as prompt injection. Its support page is blunt about where the buck stops, though: users are responsible for what Gemini does during a task, unintended purchases included.
Article Summary: Auto browse lets Gemini carry out multi-step tasks on websites by itself. Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and several other Indian languages are supported. Article Title: For every 30 Chinese AI researchers moving to the US, only one went to China; migration expert warns: The danger for the US is...
Article Text:
30 Chinese AI researchers move to US for every 1 going to China: Carnegie study

China now produces more top AI researchers than any other country

A booming home industry and travel curbs are keeping Chinese AI talent at home

South Korea and Singapore are the other big winners in the AI talent race

The US-China race for artificial intelligence is usually measured in chips and frontier models. A new study measures it in people, and the flow still runs heavily one way. For every 30 Chinese-origin AI researchers working in the United States in 2025, only one US-trained researcher was working in China, according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. In 2022, that ratio stood at 46 to one.The gap is narrowing, but slowly, and a migration expert says the headline number may be hiding the real problem. "The danger for the U.S. is a slow erosion of its appeal to attract talent that compounds over decades," said Yingyi Ma, a sociology professor at Syracuse University who studies Asian students in America. "By the time the effect shows up in the data, it is hard to reverse."Her point rests on timing. The study tracks where researchers studied and where they work now, but not when they moved. Most made that call years before the Trump administration tightened student visas, added a $100,000 fee to new H-1B petitions and cut federal research funding.For now, the US still wins the head count. The share of Chinese-origin talent among AI researchers working in America rose four percentage points to about 36%, said Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, who led the study.The US recorded a net gain of 2,145 elite researchers, while China posted a net loss of 1,729.The study, titled "Who's Ahead in the Global AI Talent Race?", follows 10,280 authors whose papers were accepted at NeurIPS 2025, one of the most selective machine learning conferences in the world. The team traced each author's undergraduate degree, graduate school and current employer, using Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to process the data with human checks at every stage.The results show how fast China's base has grown. Scientists who earned undergraduate degrees in China made up 57% of the sample, up 11 percentage points since 2022, while the US share fell to 13%. China has also overtaken the US as the top place where this talent works, at 41% against 34%.Universities tell the same story. Peking University ranked first for AI research output, followed by Tsinghua. Google, which topped the 2022 list, slipped to seventh. Twelve Chinese institutions made the top 30, double the count three years earlier.Retention is where China has gained the most. Around 69% of China-trained researchers now work in China, up from 57% in 2022, though that still trails the US at 89%.Part of the pull is prestige. Kevin Xu, founder of hedge fund Interconnected Capital, said a job at DeepSeek now carries the same professional weight as one at OpenAI, a big shift from five years ago.Part of it is control. Beijing barred the two founders of Manus from leaving the country after Meta agreed to buy the startup, and later ordered the deal unwound. Last month, reports said travel curbs on top AI and chip executives at private firms had been widened to require government approval even for short trips by their spouses and children.China has also tried to court outsiders, launching a K visa for young STEM graduates in October 2025. It has not worked so far. Only 118 researchers trained elsewhere moved to work in China, per the study. Returnees remain rare, though Tencent's hiring of former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu as chief AI scientist stood out.Away from the two superpowers, smaller Asian hubs are pulling ahead. South Korea keeps 77% of its homegrown AI researchers, the second-highest retention rate after the US. KAIST jumped 12 places to rank third among the top 30 institutions.Singapore has become a magnet of its own. It posted a net gain of 218 researchers, second only to America, and many of those arrivals came from China. National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University both broke into the top 20, while Europe's ETH Zurich and Oxford dropped off the list altogether.Which brings the story back to the 30-to-one figure. It reflects choices made before the visa crackdown, and on that count America remains the clear winner. Whether the next cohort chooses the same way is what the data cannot show yet.
Article Summary: China now produces more top AI researchers than any other country. For every 30 Chinese-origin AI researchers working in the U.S. in 2025, only one US-trained researcher was working in China. South Korea and Singapore are the other big winners in the AI talent race.

Article Title: Priscilla Chan founded a school, 10 years later, Board voted to close it; shutdown shows what philanthropic investment means for community when it arrives, and when it leaves
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan

Why the school founded by Priscilla Chan came to a closure

Academic results were mixed

The funding problem

Impact on famalies

A decade after Mark Zuckerberg’s wife Priscilla Chan launched a tuition-free private school aimed at supporting low-income children and their families, the ambitious education project has closed, highlighting both the impact and fragility of philanthropy-backed community institutions. According to a report by the Wall Street Journal, the Primary School, co-founded by Chan and funded majorly through the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), shut its doors un June after receiving more than $125 million in funding over roughly a decade. Located on East Palo Alto, California, the school opened in 2016 with a mission that went beyond academics. It sought to support the ‘whole child’ by offering services such as free dental care, development screenings, wellness coaching for parents and other support programmes often unavailable via traditional public schools.The school's board voted unanimously in April 2025 to close it after the 2025-26 academic year. People familiar with the matter told the Journal the vote followed word that CZI would not fund the school beyond that year. Board president Jean-Claude Brizard, a former head of Chicago's public schools, said he gave CZI several options beforehand, including winding down. He said the board would not have voted to close without the funder's alignment.A CZI spokesperson said the decision belonged to the board and that the organization was focused on academic results rather than cost.The decision came as CZI was narrowing its focus. Staff were told early last year that funding for social advocacy had been wound down to fit the organization's identity as a science philanthropy and the current legal and policy landscape. CZI said there was no evidence that Zuckerberg and Chan's attendance at President Trump's inauguration influenced the board's vote. Brizard called the timing an "unfortunate coincidence. "Academic results were mixed. A Stanford University report found that in spring 2025, 26% of Primary School students in third grade and above exceeded literacy standards. That compared with 14% of other local students and 47% statewide. The school said its eighth-graders, many of whom had attended for a decade, reached above 50% grade-level proficiency in their final year. Outside the classroom, the school pointed to stronger results. About 85% of its students had an annual well-child visit, against 55% of Medicaid-enrolled children in the county. Three in four students spoke a language other than English at home.Former staff described growing pains, including high principal turnover and initially unclear approaches to special education and discipline. A consultant who worked with the school said new schools can take about five years to find their footing. Some features felt more like a startup than a school: teachers signed nondisclosure agreements, and some toddlers wore recording devices at home as part of a language-development program.CZI said it had never planned to be the school's sole backer indefinitely, and had hoped the model could be sustained mainly through public investment. Chan lobbied her network for other donors, the organization said. Brizard said that was a hard sell, since donors wondered why they should fund something already supported by one of the world's wealthiest people.He also acknowledged a communication gap. The school "was never supposed to be just a philanthropic play in perpetuity," he said, adding that this may not have been articulated well enough.About 540 children were enrolled across two campuses. Ravenswood City Elementary School District is now preparing for an enrollment surge and is renovating a campus to avoid putting students in portable trailers.CZI pledged $50 million when the closure was announced. The money covers the remaining lease payments to the district and supports local groups carrying on some of the school's services. CZI also put $3.6 million into education savings accounts: $10,000 for each elementary student, $2,500 for preschoolers and $1,000 for children in early-childhood programs.Some parents said the news came too abruptly. Angelica Cardenas, 29, who has a daughter at the school and five relatives' children enrolled, said she learned of the closure from the news. She said families should have been told earlier. Mele Fakapelea, whose oldest daughter was in the founding class and who later enrolled four younger children, called the loss of the school's support system "crushing."Every teacher returned for the final year. School leaders helped families arrange tours of other schools, complete applications and open the savings accounts.In June, the school's only class of eighth-graders graduated. Fakapelea's 13-year-old daughter was one of two student speakers, and her family draped her in leis afterward.
Article Summary: The Primary School, co-founded by Chan and funded majorly through the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), shut its doors un June after receiving more than $125 million in funding over roughly a decade. It sought to support the ‘whole child’ by offering services such as free dental care, development screenings, wellness coaching for parents and other support programmes.

Jeff Bezos’ personal connection to Montessori-inspired early education

Bezos Academy recently opened its largest preschool in Texas, Bezos Academy Denton. Founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos in 2020, Bezos Academy offers Montessori-inspired preschool education at no cost to eligible families. The Denton school will also support children from across the community, including children of Texas Woman’s University (TWU) students and employees. The preschool was built on university-owned land through a partnership between TWU, Bezos Academy and the City of Denton. Families interested in future opportunities can check the academy’s website for eligibility and enrollment information.With the Denton opening, Bezos Academy now has 12 schools across Texas: six in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, five in the greater Houston area and one in San Antonio.Jeff Bezos’ focus on Montessori-inspired early education also has a personal connection. He has often spoken about how deeply his grandparents, particularly his maternal grandfather, influenced him during his formative years. His childhood experience has shaped his belief in the importance of early learning and the role supportive adults can play in a child’s development. The Bezos Academy preschool brings that idea into practice, offering Montessori-inspired education to young children while placing the school inside a senior-living community, where interaction between children and older adults can benefit both generations.
Article Summary: Bezos Academy recently opened its largest preschool in Texas, Bezos Academy Denton. Article Title: In 1992, Larry Ellison shattered his elbow in a bicycle crash; after a UC Davis surgeon repaired it, the Oracle co-founder gave $5 million to help others with bone and muscle disorders
Article Text:
Oracle founder Larry Ellison

Record-setting donation made by Larry Ellison

What the money built

A serious bicycle accident suffered by Oracle CEO Larry Ellison in the early 1990s ultimately resulted in a $5 million donation that helped expand research into bone and muscle disorders at UC Davis, according to the university. The Oracle co-founder's gift helped build a musculoskeletal research and care program at UC Davis that is still part of the university's orthopaedic identity. Ellison, the co-founder and longtime chief executive of Oracle, shattered his elbow in a bicycle crash in 1992. The injury was treated by Michael Chapman, an orthopaedic surgeon at UC Davis, who successfully reconstructed the damaged joint. Following the surgery, Ellison donated $5 million to support musculoskeletal research and patient care at the university.The gift helped establish what became the Lawrence J. Ellison Musculoskeletal Research Center, where physicians, surgeons and scientists work on research aimed at preventing and treating musculoskeletal disorders. According to UC Davis, the centre focuses on conditions affecting bones, muscles and joints, bringing together experts from multiple disciplines.UC Davis announced the pledge in September 1995, when it reported record private giving of $41.5 million for fiscal year 1994-95.That was a 39 percent increase over the $29.8 million raised the year before. Ellison, then CEO of Oracle, made the largest single gift of the year. The $5 million pledge was meant to create three endowed chairs and a musculoskeletal institute in the School of Medicine."Mr. Ellison's generosity in particular will help sustain our nationally recognized expertise and care for patients with bone or muscle diseases," said Gerald S. Lazarus, then dean of the School of Medicine. The School of Medicine received $12.7 million in private support that year, an 88 percent increase. The university said this was the largest amount ever given to an academic unit on the campus.The Ellison center brings together physicians, surgeons and basic scientists. They study the prevention and treatment of what UC Davis calls "crippling and painful musculoskeletal disorders."A 2011 UC Davis Health profile described the center as part of a broader orthopaedic and sports medicine program. Its specialists have served as team doctors for the NBA's Sacramento Kings for more than two decades. The same program provides care for Olympic-level athletes, the national soccer program and UC Davis teams. US News & World Report ranked UC Davis among the nation's best hospitals for orthopaedics.Paul Di Cesare, then chair of orthopaedic surgery, said the program uses the same advanced techniques for professionals and ordinary patients. "We use those same modalities and treatments for the average athlete and the weekend warrior," he said.
Article Summary: Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison shattered his elbow in a bicycle crash in 1992. Ellison donated $5 million to support musculoskeletal research and patient care at UC Davis. The gift helped establish what became the Lawrence J. Ellison Musculo-Oriental Research Center.

Article Title: Claude Code creator Boris Cherny shares what not to miss while giving prompt to Claude; says: There's no secret to ...
Article Text:
Anthropic’s Boris Cherny reveals what matters on prompting AI today

The prompt that caught attention

Anthropic’s Claude Code creator, Boris Cherny has offered a simple piece of advice to users who are trying to get better results from AI models. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cherny asked the users to talk to Claude the same way they would talk to a coworker. As per Cherny users no longer need highly structured and very detailed prompts for most tasks, as modern AI models are increasingly capable of figuring out how to achieve a goal on their own. In the post shared on X, Cherny revealed that he was surprised that people were surprised by the way he prompts Claude. “Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks. Give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out,” he wrote.Cherny contrasted the current approach with the early days of Claude's Sonnet 3.5 models, when the exact wording of a prompt mattered a great deal. Today's models, he suggested, need less hand-holding on the "how" and more clarity about the "what."He said it is now much more important to communicate three things to the model:1. What you want it to do2. How much effort you want it to spend3. How it should verify that it did the right thingThe comments align with advice Cherny has shared in public discussions, where he has argued that many users make the mistake of over-specifying every step instead of clearly defining the desired outcome.Modern AI models are often better used by describing the goal and success criteria rather than dictating a rigid sequence of actions.Alongside his comments, Cherny shared an example of a prompt he uses with Claude.In the example, he asked the AI to create an interactive artefact about a recent podcast episode on Home Depot's acquisition strategy. Rather than providing detailed step-by-step instructions, he described the end goal: a visually rich, interactive experience that highlights key business lessons.The prompt asked Claude to make the output “beautiful and interactive,” focus on business wisdom from the episode, use extensive reasoning and iteration, and incorporate elements such as watercolour illustrations, historical photographs and visual storytelling inspired by publications such as The New Yorker and The New York Times.Notably, the prompt emphasised the desired outcome and quality bar rather than prescribing a detailed process, reflecting the prompting philosophy Cherny advocates.
Article Summary: Anthropic’s Claude Code creator, Boris Cherny has offered a simple piece of advice to users who are trying to get better results from AI models. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cherny asked the users to talk to Claude the same way they would talk to a coworker.

Article Title: AI Data Security : Everyone wants an AI agent but almost nobody is asking where the data goes
Article Text:
Start with some very simple questions

“Trust us” isn’t enough

AI needs to earn our trust

By: Krish Ramineni, Co-founder & CEO, Fireflies.ai

Everyone wants an AI agent right now. We want AI that can prepare us for meetings, answer emails, search through our work, update the CRM and eventually just get things done for us. That’s where this is going. AI is moving from something you open when you need help to something that is always there, working alongside you. Less like another tool and more like an AI teammate.But there’s one question we’re not asking enough: Where does all that data go?Because the more useful your AI teammate becomes, the more it needs to know about you and your company. If it’s preparing you for a meeting, it might need access to your calendar, past meetings and documents. If it’s writing an email, it might need access to your inbox. If it’s updating your CRM, it needs access to customer information. And if you eventually want it doing work for you all day, it may need access to almost everything you use at work. The most useful AI teammate may also be the one that knows the most about your work. That’s why security matters so much.Before a company gives an AI access to its information, it should know what happens to that information. Is our data being used to train AI models? Where is it stored? How long is it kept? Who can see it? Can we delete it? Can we control what the AI has access to? Can we see what actions it has taken? And what happens when another AI company or model is involved?These sound like basic questions. But as we give AI access to more of our work, they become incredibly important.Security shouldn’t be something companies think about after they buy an AI product. It should be part of deciding which AI products they trust in the first place.Microsoft says Copilot follows a company’s existing permissions and that its business data isn’t used to train its foundation models. Google says Gemini for Workspace follows existing Workspace protections and doesn’t use customer data to train its generative AI models without permission. Zoom says it doesn’t use customer communications to train its own or third-party AI models. There’s a reason companies are starting to make these promises much clearer. Security is becoming part of the product.This becomes even more important when AI has access to conversations. Think about what gets discussed in meetings: customers, employees, hiring, strategy, financials and plans that may never be written down anywhere else. Companies should know exactly what happens to that information. At Fireflies, for example, we don’t use customer meeting content to train AI models. We require third-party vendors handling meeting content to follow zero-data-retention requirements. We also maintain SOC 2 Type II, GDPR and HIPAA compliance. “Trust us” isn’t a security policy. Companies should be able to understand where their data goes, who can access it and what controls they have over it.Banning AI isn’t the answer. Some companies may look at these risks and decide the safest thing to do is block AI altogether. I don’t think that solves the problem. People are already using AI to write, research, prepare for meetings and get work done faster. If their company blocks these tools, some employees will simply use personal accounts or other apps the company doesn’t know about. Now the company has even less control over where its data is going.A better approach is to give employees AI products the company has actually reviewed and approved and then set clear rules around what those products can see and what they’re allowed to do.This gets even more important as AI starts taking action. There’s a big difference between drafting an email and sending it. There’s a difference between suggesting a CRM update and making the change. There’s a difference between finding a document and sharing it with someone.The more AI can do on your behalf, the more control you need over what it’s allowed to do.For the last few years, everyone has been focused on making AI smarter. Can it answer better questions? Can it understand more? Can it do more work?Those things still matter. But as AI becomes more deeply connected to our work, there’s another question that matters just as much: Can we trust it?Today, a company might use AI to take meeting notes. Tomorrow, that same AI teammate could prepare you for meetings, search your email and Slack, update your CRM, follow up with customers and take care of work across dozens of apps.Every time we give it another ability, we’re also giving it more access. And that means companies need to know that their AI teammate is looking at the right information, for the right reason, and doing only what it has permission to do.The goal isn’t just to build AI that knows more. It’s to build AI that we can trust to do more.
Article Summary: AI is moving from something you open when you need help to something that is always there. “Trust us” isn’t a security policy. Companies should be able to understand where their data goes, who can access it and what controls they have over it.

EmbeddingGemma 2: Key capabilities

Superior code understanding: Significantly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1 on code search and technical retrieval, making it ideal for local codebase indexing and agentic code search.

Modular memory footprint: Selectively load only the encoders you need at runtime: 270M (text/code), 440M (text + vision), 570M (text + audio), or 740M (full multimodal), all projecting into the same compatible vector space.

Flexible vector storage: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) enables dynamic truncation from 768 dimensions down to 128 dimensions, cutting vector database storage requirements while retaining much of the original quality. For instance, at 256 dimensions, most of the full quality of the original embedding on text and code is retained and about 95% on image, video, and speech retrieval

How it works

Text and code (270M base): An adapted Gemma 4 decoder with an 8,192-token context window.

Vision (+170M): A vision encoder that processes images, visual documents (PDFs, slides, charts), and video frames.

Audio (+300M): A dedicated speech and sound encoder that directly ingests raw audio.

Modular loading: You only load what you need. Run text-only at 270M parameters, add vision for 440M parameters, or load the full multimodal model at 740M parameters.

Shared tokenizer & audio encoder with Gemma 4: When paired with Gemma 4 in an on-device RAG pipeline, both models share the same text tokenizer and audio encoder architecture, reducing the total memory footprint.

Google has launched EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model for devices. The launch comes a year after the company introduced EmbeddingGemma for developers last year. For those unaware, an embedding model is a machine learning tool that turns complex data like words, sentences, images, or audio into a list of numbers called a vector. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license, EmbeddingGemma 2 has 740 million parameters, making it optimal for on-device inference. It can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model.EmbeddingGemma 2 is designed to provide a single, compact open model released under the Apache 2.0 license, delivering exceptional multimodal performance for its size. Based on Gemma 4, this sub-1B model maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Its modular architecture can scale from 270M parameters for text and code up to 740M parameters for all modalities.
