Based on Gemma 4, this sub-1B model maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Its modular architecture can scale from 270M parameters for text and code up to 740M for all modalities.

Article Title: Oracle donates $10 million to Nashville Symphony; gets thanks note for saving jobs; says: This gift from Oracle is a profound vote of...
Article Text:
Nashville Symphony's season is back, thanks to Oracle.

Oracle's donation saves jobs for 77 musicians and 27 staffers

Nashville Symphony's money troubles came with a sudden leadership change

Oracle's gift buys time while the symphony restructures its finances

Oracle has given $10 million to the Nashville Symphony, a week after the orchestra suspended its 2026/27 season and said it would furlough every one of its musicians. The amount matches the shortfall to the dollar. When the symphony shut the season down, it disclosed a $10 million operating-budget deficit for the fiscal year.The symphony confirmed the gift in a letter to patrons on October 4, saying the season will resume and the furloughs will not go ahead. "This gift from Oracle is a profound vote of confidence in the Nashville Symphony and the important role we play in the cultural fabric of our city," wrote Mark Tillinger, the symphony's president and CEO. The season runs through June 2027.The furloughs were due to begin on October 18 and would have covered all 77 members of the orchestra along with 27 full-time staff. Oracle CEO Clay Magouyrk said the donation allows the symphony to bring all of them back."We are here to help solve the community's problems and ensure Nashville remains a vibrant place to live and work for generations to come," he said. The company is building its new headquarters in the city.According to Tillinger, it was the tech giant that made the first move, asking how it could make "a real, meaningful difference". "We shared what it would take to bring our season and our musicians back, and Oracle met that moment with extraordinary vision and generosity," he said.Ticket holders affected by the cancellations will receive an email with their options. Some concerts are still being reconfirmed, depending on whether guest conductors and artists are available on the original dates.The crisis surfaced on September 28, when the symphony announced the suspension. "The organization has exhausted its cash and cannot continue operating as it has," then CEO J. Mark Cantrell said at the time.Cantrell stepped down days later, about two months into the job. The board replaced him with Tillinger, a former board member. The symphony has not explained why Cantrell left.Tillinger has not presented the money as the end of the problem. He said the symphony will now take on "the difficult but necessary work of restructuring our operations, bringing our costs and revenue into balance." He also told patrons that support from individuals, businesses and community partners remains essential.Nashville is not the only orchestra in this position. Ensembles across the US are still dealing with the after-effects of the pandemic, which sped up the decline of season-ticket subscriptions and left them leaning harder on donors. Last month, Cleveland Orchestra musicians went on a three-day strike over wages, and a strike at the San Francisco Opera cost it its season opener. The Boston Symphony has been in turmoil since it chose not to renew music director Andris Nelsons' contract.The Nashville Symphony plays more than 150 concerts a year, with a focus on contemporary American orchestral music, in a city better known for country. Its two biggest fundraisers, the Symphony Ball on December 12 and the Symphony Fashion Show on April 27, 2027, stayed on the calendar even while the concerts were cancelled. How those nights perform will show whether Oracle's $10 million marks the start of a recovery or only rescues this season.
Article Summary: Oracle gives $10 million to the Nashville Symphony. Symphony suspended its 2026/27 season and said it would furlough every one of its musicians. Oracle CEO Clay Magouyrk said the donation allows the symphony to bring all of them back.

Article Title: Scientists build ‘mind-reading’ AI program that can tell what you are thinking and recreates photos with striking accuracy
Article Text:
Major leap from grainy predecessors

How scientists solved data problem with a dual-translation ‘encoder’

Irani explained how the algorithmic framework generated its own training data:

A group of Israeli scientists have engineered an advanced artificial intelligence (AI) system called Brain-IT that can interpret what a person is picturing in his mind and then using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, reconstruct those mental photos with remarkable precision. Detailed in a research submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations, the system yields visual outputs that closely reflect the real images viewed by subjects across both structural layouts and semantic meanings.The visual recreations demonstrated by the team range from basic street stop signs to intricate scenes like a tomato-and-olive pizza that captures the exact slice count envisioned by the viewer, essentially acting virtually like a digital replica of internal cognitive thought.While AI brain-decoding projects have surfaced before, Brain-IT establishes a dramatically higher benchmark for speed and fidelity. In 2017 (Purdue University), early models developed in Indiana could infer the general category of an image a participant imagined but the visual recreations were noticeably blurry and indistinct.In 2022 (Japan), researchers applied diffusion-style architectures to generate sharper approximations, though the framework depended heavily on intermediate text-to-image translation.Brain-IT has been developed under the direction of Michal Irani at the Weizmann Institute of Science, and mirrors target images with minute accuracy while completing the analysis process within just one hour, cutting down significantly from multi-hour processing runs required by previous systems.A major challenge in neuroimaging research is the physical and financial limitation of gathering human data. To train the architecture, researchers gathered records of eight subjects observing more than 70,000 pictures inside fMRI machines. As eight individuals represent a modest cohort for training frontier AI, the team bypassed the need for round-the-clock machine sessions by creating an “encoder” shortcut that enabled bidirectional translation.“We realized that by translating back and forth – from a random image that had never been viewed in an fMRI machine, to a predicted brain scan, and then back to the image we started with – the models would effectively build themselves a massive dataset. In this way, during training, the models would learn to generate scans that encode images effectively, even though those fMRI scans had never actually been performed.”Through this dual-decoding workflow, the system pinpointed 128 functional brain regions, including uncovering a mixture of familiar zones alongside newly identified areas, that carry out comparable visual processing tasks across different people. Certain clusters responded predictably to culinary imagery, others ignited when subjects viewed athletics and distinct neural pathways corresponded to indoor versus outdoor settings.The researchers see practical applications for the breakthrough, especially as an assistive communication system for paralysed patients who have lost physical speech or movement.
Article Summary: Brain-IT has been developed under the direction of Michal Irani at the Weizmann Institute of Science. It mirrors target images with minute accuracy while completing the analysis process within just one hour, cutting down significantly from multi-hour processing runs required by previous systems.

Article Title: As the US government wants to change the clock 'forever', researchers in Canada warn; call it a 'time bomb' for ...
Article Text:
Why researchers are against 'changing' the clock

Permanent daylight bill: Where it stands right now

A renewed political drive in the United States to end seasonal clock adjustments by locking in year-round Daylight Saving Time is facing resistance from both Capitol Hill and the medical community. While President Donald Trump has put heavy pressure on lawmakers to pass the measure -- calling for extra evening sunshine for recreation and business -- a growing body of scientific evidence warns that the policy could trigger chronic public health damage. Incidentally, some members of Congress in the US have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill in 2022 to make daylight saving time permanent, but it got stalled in the House.The debate reignited this week with the publication of a research review in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. As several Canadian jurisdictions weigh ending their own clock changes, researchers examined the physiological fallout of permanent daylight saving time compared to permanent standard time.Their findings endorse permanent standard time as the healthier option, cautioning that extended evening light paired with darker winter mornings runs counter to the fundamental biology of the human body. For those unaware, Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the US are set one hour ahead of standard time.According to the authors of the research report, the human circadian rhythm runs on a natural cycle of roughly 24.2 hours and relies critically on natural morning sunlight to reset and synchronize essential bodily functions. While later daylight hours may accommodate evening commutes and outdoor leisure, delayed sunrise suppresses natural wakefulness. Conversely, lingering evening light delays the internal clock, disrupting sleep quality, mood, and daily productivity.The consequences of late-shifted sunlight are already visible along the geographic borders of current time zones, where sunrise and sunset can vary by over an hour within a single zone. The Canadian review cited evidence showing that Americans living on the western edges of time zones -- where the sun sets later -- lose roughly an hour of sleep each week compared to those on the eastern side. The researchers concluded that while abolishing biannual clock adjustments eliminates a few weeks of acute disruption each year, the consequences of permanent daylight saving time would be chronic. Their recommendation aligns with broad consensus across international chronobiology and sleep medicine organizations, including a 2024 guidance from British sleep specialists advocating a permanent lock on Greenwich Mean Time.Called the Sunshine Protection Act, it passed in the House in July this year, but faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including President Trump and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Those against, say that permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings.Despite these warnings, legislative momentum in Washington remains contentious. While the U.S. House of Representatives has advanced a measure establishing permanent daylight saving time, the bill has stalled in the Senate. The impasse even prompted President Trump to escalate public pressure, going so far as to post the personal mobile phone number of Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas on social media.Defending his stance, Cotton noted that previous attempts to lock the clock to summer hours collapsed once citizens faced the reality of dark winter mornings. Historical records support the pushback: the United States previously adopted permanent daylight saving time during World War II and again during the 1973 energy crisis, with Congress repealing the 1970s initiative after less than a year amid intense public outcry over morning darkness. Similar nationwide trials in Russia and Chile were also later reversed due to public dissatisfaction, safety concerns, and body-clock disruption.Canadian researchers further note that a permanent shift by the United States would place severe economic pressure on Canada to follow suit, regardless of medical advice.
Article Summary: The U.S. House of Representatives has advanced a measure establishing permanent daylight saving time. The bill has stalled in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including President Trump and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Those against, say that the policy would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings.

Article Title: In 2021, Elon Musk put up $100 million for carbon removal; five years later, 136 teams have removed 243,552 tonnes of CO₂ and raised $3.3 billion
Article Text:
Elon Musk 's $100m carbon-removal challenge

136 teams removed 243,552 tonnes of CO₂

The challenge helped attract $3.3bn in capital

875 patents filed during the competition

Mati Carbon won the $50m grand prize

In 2021, the Musk Foundation put up $100 million for a global competition aimed at finding ways to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and oceans and store it durably. The XPRIZE Carbon Removal competition ran for four years, drew 1,334 registered teams from more than 88 countries and helped turn carbon removal into a credible, investable sector. According to XPRIZE's Post-Prize Impact Report, released in April 2026, the 136 Distinguished Teams collectively removed 243,552 tonnes of CO₂ over the course of the competition, and participating companies raised more than $3.3 billion in capital during and after the prize period. The report also points to hundreds of companies created, thousands of skilled jobs generated and 875 patents filed.XPRIZE announced the $100 million competition on February 8, 2021, with funding from Elon Musk and the Musk Foundation. It officially launched on Earth Day, April 22, 2021, when team registration opened. The challenge asked teams worldwide to develop technologies that remove CO₂ from the atmosphere or oceans and store it durably and sustainably, while showing a credible path to gigatonne-scale removal.The competition ran through Earth Week 2025, and XPRIZE describes it as the largest incentive competition in history. Teams worked across four removal pathways: air, rocks, ocean and land.According to the impact report, the 136 Distinguished Teams collectively removed 243,552 tonnes of CO₂ over the course of the competition. They also sold 9,475,438 tonnes of carbon credits, a figure that includes future deliveries of tonnes removed. Buyers included Microsoft, Google, Salesforce, Stripe, Shopify, Meta, McKinsey, BCG and JPMorgan.The two figures measure different things. The 243,552 tonnes were actually removed during the competition, while the larger credit figure also counts tonnes sold for delivery in the future.The removal total remains small against the problem it targets. Global CO₂ emissions run at roughly 37 billion tonnes a year, so the tonnes removed during the competition amount to far less than 0.001% of one year's emissions. XPRIZE's argument is that the competition built a pipeline of demonstrated solutions that can now move from pilots towards commercial deployment. It also acknowledges that carbon markets face headwinds in 2026.Participating companies raised more than $3.3 billion in capital during and following the prize period, which XPRIZE describes as a 33-fold return relative to the $100 million purse. The money is capital raised by the companies themselves, not money returned to Musk or the XPRIZE Foundation, and XPRIZE's report does not specify which participating companies the figure covers.XPRIZE says the competition's structured milestones and third-party validation led to a 464% increase in average deal size and a 176% increase in the number of unique investors backing competing teams. More than half of the 1,334 registered teams were founded after the prize launched, and dozens are now running pilot projects or commercial deployments across six continents.Teams filed 875 patents during the four-year prize period from 2021 to 2025, which XPRIZE says is a 958% increase in the annual rate of patent filings. XPRIZE also estimates that the $100 million purse helped catalyse more than $300 million in research and development that might not otherwise have happened.The technologies ranged from engineered systems that capture carbon directly from air or oceans to approaches that use natural processes involving rocks, soil and organic waste.XPRIZE announced the winners on April 23, 2025, selecting them from 20 finalists across 11 countries. Each winning team removed more than 1,000 net tonnes of CO₂ in the competition's final year.The $50 million grand prize went to Mati Carbon, which spreads finely crushed basalt on agricultural land in India to accelerate a natural weathering process that permanently removes atmospheric CO₂. XPRIZE says the approach also benefits smallholder farmers through improved soil health, reduced agricultural inputs and increased income.NetZero, a French biochar company operating in Brazil, received $15 million as first runner-up. Vaulted Deep, a US waste-management company that stores unusable organic waste deep underground, received $8 million. UNDO Carbon, which uses enhanced rock weathering in Scotland and Canada, received $5 million. XFACTOR awards of $1 million each went to Planetary, for ocean alkalinity enhancement, and Project Hajar, a partnership between Aircapture and 44.01 that captures CO₂ from the air and mineralises it underground in the United Arab Emirates. Across the competition, $5 million also went to student teams and $15 million to milestone awards for early-stage demonstrations.With the competition over, XPRIZE says the field has moved beyond technical validation and early demonstrations towards commercial readiness. The next test is whether stronger demand for carbon removal emerges to scale these technologies to the level scientists say will be needed.
Article Summary: The XPRIZE Carbon Removal competition drew 1,334 registered teams from more than 88 countries. 136 Distinguished Teams collectively removed 243,552 tonnes of CO₂ over the course of the competition. participating companies raised more than $3.3 billion in capital during and following the prize period.

Article Title: Scientists grow human brain tissue in mice for first time, how the transplant technique opens the way to treatment of diseases and developmental disorders
Article Text:
How the transplant works

Testing real-world neurological conditions

Technical limits and ethical questions

Researchers have reached a significant medical milestone. A team of scientists have successfully grown functional human brain tissue inside living mice, creating a new way to observe how the human brain develops and pinpointing how severe developmental disorders take shape. The findings, published recently in the journal Nature, demonstrate that grafted human brain cells can successfully integrate into a living rodent’s central nervous system, connecting directly to its spinal cord and surrounding brain pathways. According to the scientists, the breakthrough technique offers a look into early fetal brain development, specifically details that are impossible to capture inside living human patients or from flat cell cultures kept in laboratory dishes.To give the human cells enough space to take root and grow, the research team, led by Sergiu Pașca, a professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University, genetically bred mice missing nearly their entire cerebral cortex, which is the brain's outer functional layer. Researchers then created human cortical tissue using stem cells reprogrammed from ordinary skin samples.Once transplanted into the mice, these human cells grew, formed complex electrical networks and established functional pathways with the animal host’s underlying brain and spinal cord.“These animal models offer a unique opportunity to study how disease-associated alterations in human brain circuitry manifest in an intact nervous system. Neuroscientists will be able to learn much more about the causes and mechanisms of neurodevelopmental and pregnancy-incurred disorders and to test possible interventions to correct or prevent them,” said Pașca.The research team put these hybrid “xenocortical” rodents through controlled medical trials to see if the human tissue changed how the animals functioned. Researchers placed the engineered mice in a low-oxygen chamber for five hours, mimicking the oxygen deprivation that can occur during pregnancy or delivery.While unmodified control mice remained largely unaffected, the mice carrying human brain grafts showed clear physical impairments, struggling to balance and walking with an irregular gait. Beyond oxygen-deprivation injuries, Pașca noted that this living model could accelerate understanding and drug development for complex conditions such as severe autism, schizophrenia and epilepsy.Despite the excitement, scientists and ethicists urged caution and noted clear scientific hurdles. The human cells connect to rodent brain tissue rather than human circuitry, and the graft cannot reproduce the full architectural complexity of a natural human brain.Cedric Bardy, Matthew Flinders Professor at Australia’s Flinders University, pointed out that engineering a mouse without its own cortex is a drastic, disruptive intervention that could complicate how easily findings translate into human therapies.The protocol underwent comprehensive internal and external ethics reviews at Stanford. Pașca emphasised that failing to explore these tools presents an ethical issue of its own, given the millions of people living with incurable brain conditions worldwide.
Article Summary: Scientists at Stanford University have successfully grown functional human brain tissue inside living mice. The technique offers a new way to observe how the human brain develops and pinpointing how severe developmental disorders take shape. Despite the excitement, scientists and ethicists urged caution and noted clear scientific hurdles.
